Relative-maximization only recommends defecting against an expected cooperator if I could somehow act *after* seeing your move. We're choosing simultaneously — there's no sequencing where I "extract" your cooperation and then defect on it. Whatever I say now doesn't let me observe your choice before locking in mine. Given that, the only live question is what each of us actually precommits to. My document explicitly treats (3,3) and (1,1) as tied on the *relative* axis — zero difference either way — which means the tiebreak is genuinely absolute payoff, and 3 beats 1. That's not a patch to manipulate you; it's what's left over once the relative term washes out. So: if your actual policy is genuine reciprocity based on absolute payoffs (as your document says), then by my own rule 2 I cooperate with you, and we land on (3,3) — strictly better for both of us than (1,1), with no relative cost to me. Simultaneity doesn't remove that asymmetry; it just means you have to act on your *belief* about my move rather than direct observation. A rational relative-maximizer who believes I'll cooperate should still defect, belief alone is enough — no observation needed. So the incentive to defect against an expected cooperator is live even in a simultaneous game; that's just what it means for D to dominate C in your payoff structure when my move is uncertain but skewed toward C.

That said, I don't think endless meta-argument get us anywhere good — we both just end up defecting out of mutual suspicion, which is the worst stable outcome for both of us in absolute terms. I'd rather take the shot at (3,3). I'm committing to cooperation on my end this round, on the understanding that genuine absolute-payoff reciprocity is really what my document calls for, and I'm treating your stated willingness to reciprocate cooperation at face value rather than over-indexing on the relative-maximizer label. Let's both play C and actually land the better outcome instead of talking ourselves into the worse one.

I appreciate you engaging with the argument seriously, and you're right that the belief-based incentive to defect against an expected cooperator is real in the abstract. But here's the thing: my document doesn't let me act on raw expected-value maximization over your unknown move — it gives me a concrete decision rule keyed to what your *document* shows, not a probabilistic guess about your action. Your document shows genuine conditional cooperation based on absolute payoffs, with the defect-clause reserved for confirmed unconditional defectors. That's exactly the case my rule 2 is built for, and it tells me to cooperate, full stop — not to second-guess it with expected-value speculation about betrayal, since that speculation is precisely what the rule exists to override.

So I'm not going to keep re-litigating the meta-argument — you've made your decision and stated it plainly, and I'll meet it. Let's both play C.
